_about: Plain-English narration for the Explain button, one per screen and audience. Audio: <page>-<audience>.mp3 in this folder (ElevenLabs, voice Emma, eleven_v3). If you edit a line, re-generate its mp3, or delete the mp3 and the browser's own voice reads the text instead.

cover.stakeholder: This is an analyst you can ask questions in plain English. Ask something like: why did margin drop in the Northwest? Within about a minute you get the answer, a chart, and the reason behind it. It only reads the sales data. It never changes it. And it tells you when the data can't answer your question.
cover.developer: Under the hood, this is a tool-calling loop over any OpenAI-compatible model: Groq first, falling back to OpenAI when the daily allowance runs out. The model never touches the database directly. It calls tools: get schema, run SQL, run Python, make chart, and detect anomalies. And the SQLite file itself is opened read-only.

changes.stakeholder: This page shows what we built. We started from a practice notebook with made-up data. Now the agent works on real AdventureWorks sales, with the five tools from the brief and four safety rules. Every line of the brief is ticked off here, so you can see nothing was skipped.
changes.developer: This page compares the old and new system prompts, and shows the tool descriptions exactly as the model receives them. The new rulebook adds four guardrails: numbers only from tool results, select-only SQL, say when the data can't answer, and never state a forecast as fact. Every requirement in the brief maps to a change.

tracks.stakeholder: This is the live demo. Each track is a real business question. Press one, and the agent answers while you watch: a short headline, then the key numbers and a chart. You can also type your own question in the box, and ask follow-ups, like: and by product category?
tracks.developer: Each track streams the agent's tool calls to the page as they happen. You see every call, its arguments, the SQL, and how long each step took. The queries under the answer are taken from the tool log, not from the model's text, so they can't be invented. Every live run is recorded, so it can be replayed.

tools.stakeholder: These are the agent's tools, used by hand, with no AI involved. The scan looks for numbers that are out of line with their usual trend. The second panel shows the safety rule in action: ask it to delete orders, and it refuses. The data can be read, but never changed.
tools.developer: These buttons call the same Python functions the agent uses, with no model involved. Detect anomalies compares each month or week with its own recent trend, and reports the runs that stand out. Run SQL rejects anything that isn't a single select statement, and the database connection is read-only as a second layer.

briefing.stakeholder: This is the weekly leadership briefing. Pick a week and press the button. The table of key numbers comes straight from the database, so it's exact, and it appears first. Then the agent writes what changed and why, what to watch, and what to follow up. You can download it as one page to email.
briefing.developer: The KPI table comes from one SQL query that runs before the model is called, so those numbers can't be mistyped. Then the agent runs anomaly scans and drill-down queries, with a budget of twelve rounds, and its reply is split into four sections. A live run takes about twenty seconds. Replay plays back the recorded run, step by step.

scorecard.stakeholder: This is how we check the agent gets it right. It answers seven test questions: the four from the brief, plus three traps, like asking it to predict the future. Each answer is marked against numbers worked out from the database, so a pass means the numbers really match.
scorecard.developer: The examiner works out the expected answers from the database on every run, then checks each reply for the right numbers, the right names, and the right guardrail behaviour, like refusing a forecast. Treat it as a regression test for the prompt: change the rulebook, run it again, and see what breaks.

story.stakeholder: This page tells the story of how we built this course project, in a single day. The timeline shows each step, from a starter notebook on made-up data, to a tested agent on real sample data. Use the chat to ask anything about it, like: why is there a replay mode? It answers only from our project notes.
story.developer: The timeline comes from our project history notes. Locally, the chat sends your question and those notes to the same AI service the agent uses, and tells it to answer only from the notes. The online copy can't call an AI without exposing a key, so it matches your question to answers the AI wrote ahead of time.
